issues.legal_issue: A challenge to statutory compensation provisions as a colourable exercise of legislative power under the earlier constitutional framework cannot be entertained when that framework contained no corresponding legislative entry and the current Constitution makes the earlier compensation guarantee unavailable.
material_facts: The holder of an estate and an under-tenure challenged proceedings under a land-abolition statute in constitutional writ petitions, which the High Court dismissed.
The challenge alleged that the statute’s compensation provisions were a colourable exercise of legislative power under the Government of India Act, 1935.
The appellant pointed out that no compensation had been allowed for a large number of under-tenures.
The Court treated the issue as governed by its decision in Zamindar of Ettayapuram v. State of Madras.
issues.conclusion: The challenge could not be entertained because the former legislative lists contained no entry corresponding to the relevant entry in the present Constitution and the earlier compensation guarantee was unavailable under Article 31(6). The appeal was dismissed without an order as to costs.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Zamindar of Ettayapuram v. State of Madras, AIR 1954 SC 257, the Court held that the absence in the Government of India Act, 1935 of an entry corresponding to Entry 42 of List III of the Constitution meant the appellant could not raise the challenge on that basis, and Article 31(6) made the guarantee in Section 299(2) of the 1935 Act unavailable. The asserted absence of compensation for some under-tenures did not permit relief.

issues.definition: When a claimant brings a constitutional writ appeal challenging compensation legislation as a colourable exercise of power, and the earlier legislative lists lack a corresponding entry while the earlier compensation guarantee is unavailable, the challenge cannot be entertained.
